messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Known People: Related people, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi Patel is a 49-year-old military medic who came to treatment after months of telling himself that what happened at home should not be affecting him the way it does. He is married, and when he first speaks about the abuse, he does so haltingly, circling around it as if language itself fails him. He can describe pieces with precision—the smell of sweat trapped in fabric, the sound of a voice at close range, the pressure and impact on his body—but when asked to tell the whole event from beginning to end, he loses the thread and says he cannot seem to put it into words. What emerges over the first sessions is that the abuse came from his romantic partner during a volatile confrontation in their home. The assault was physical and intimate in a way that left him feeling cornered and degraded. He remembers being close enough to register his partner’s body odor and sweat, remembers the clothes worn that day vividly enough that he later stopped wearing similar ones himself, and remembers pain in specific parts of his body that still returns with the memory. The fact that this happened inside a marriage, in a place that should have been safe, has remained especially hard for him to absorb.

In the immediate aftermath, Ravi did what he had long done as a medic and as a soldier: he kept moving, minimized, and tried to contain it. But the experience did not settle into the past. When it comes back, it does not feel like recollection. He says there are moments when he is no longer merely remembering but is back in that room, with the same bodily alarm and the same sense of being trapped. At those times he feels pain in the same areas that were hurt during the assault, as if his body is repeating the event even when his mind is trying not to. The smell of sweat on another person, especially in enclosed spaces, can bring this on abruptly. So can seeing people connected to his partner or the relationship. Even the presence of police has become charged. He does not describe this abstractly; he describes scanning parking lots, stiffening when a police cruiser is nearby, and feeling his chest tighten at the sight of uniforms or official authority, as if exposure to them means being pulled into something dangerous and uncontrollable again. Underneath this is a bitter conviction that the people responsible have faced no consequences.

These reactions have narrowed his life. He has begun avoiding clothes that resemble what he wore during the assault, passing over certain shirts without fully explaining why even to himself at first. He no longer exercises, despite having once depended on physical training as part of military life. The combination of exertion, sweat, and heightened bodily sensation feels intolerable to him now. He also avoids people. At work and outside it, he keeps interactions brief and functional, withdrawing from colleagues and limiting contact with anyone who might ask personal questions. As a medic, he still moves through settings full of noise, urgency, and close human contact, and this has become increasingly difficult. Ordinary sounds that others barely register make him jump. A slammed door, a piece of equipment dropping, or a sudden voice nearby can cause an immediate startle response that leaves him embarrassed and angry with himself. He has come to feel safe only in a very limited number of places, and even there he struggles to settle. At night he has difficulty falling asleep because he feels he must stay alert. Sleep seems to require surrender, and surrender feels unsafe.

Over time, Ravi’s interpretation of himself has grown harsh and despairing. He has come to believe there is something wrong with him as a person, though he struggles to say exactly what. The fact that he cannot simply master this privately feels, to him, like evidence of defectiveness rather than injury. He speaks with particular pain about meaning draining out of his life. Work had once given him a clear identity, and marriage had once anchored him; now both feel altered. He still goes through the motions of duty, but he says nothing feels meaningful anymore.

What finally brought him to seek help was not one dramatic crisis but an accumulation he could no longer ignore: increasing isolation, persistent sleeplessness, and the sense that his world had contracted to a few “safe” places and rigid routines. He began to recognize that he was arranging entire days around what to avoid—the wrong clothes, other people, exercise, certain encounters at work—while feeling constantly on edge anyway. Coming to treatment, he is ashamed, guarded, and deeply skeptical that talking will help when the event itself remains so hard to narrate. At the same time, he is hoping for some relief from the immediacy of the memories and from the conviction that his life has lost its meaning. What frightens him most is the possibility that this is now permanent: that he will remain alert, hemmed in, and inwardly marked by something he still cannot fully say aloud.
